blocks.text: While Aeneas was away finding friends, Turnus attacked the Trojan camp by the river. The Trojans shut the gates and fought from their walls, as Aeneas had told them. The enemy soldiers locked their shields together over their heads, like the shell of a tortoise, and crept up to the walls. The Trojans rolled down huge rocks to smash the shields apart.

In that battle, young Ascanius shot his first arrow at an enemy. A boastful warrior named Numanus was strutting in front of the walls, shouting insults. "You Trojans are soft!" he jeered. "You like dancing and pretty clothes. We Italians are tough. We dip our newborn babies in cold streams to make them strong!"

Ascanius had only ever hunted animals. But he would not let anyone insult his people. He prayed to Jupiter, drew his bow and let the arrow fly. It hit Numanus, and the boaster spoke no more. Then the god Apollo came down to Ascanius, disguised as an old servant. "Well done, young hero," he said. "But that is enough battle for you today."

Meanwhile, Aeneas was sailing back down the coast with his new friends, the Etruscans, in a great fleet of ships. In the night, a group of sea nymphs came swimming alongside his ship. They had once been his own Trojan ships. When Turnus had tried to burn them, the gods had turned them into nymphs, and now they swam the seas. "Hurry, Aeneas," they said. "Your son and your people are in danger." And they gave his ship a push to send it on its way.

When the sun rose, the Trojans on their walls saw Aeneas standing at the front of his ship, holding up his new shield. It flashed like fire in the morning light. The Trojans gave a great shout of joy.

Then came a fierce battle on the beach. Aeneas fought like a hero. Young Pallas fought bravely too, leading his horsemen. But Turnus came to fight him. Pallas was brave, but Turnus was older and much stronger. And Pallas fell. Turnus took his gold-studded belt and put it on, as a prize. It was a cruel thing to do, and one day he would be sorry for it.

When Aeneas heard that Pallas had fallen, he was filled with grief and anger. He thought of old King Evander, who had trusted him with his only son. He fought his way across the battlefield, looking for Turnus. But Juno did not want Turnus to die. So she made a ghost that looked just like Aeneas, and it ran away from Turnus, and Turnus chased it onto a ship. Then Juno cut the ship loose and let it drift out to sea, carrying Turnus far away from the battle, shouting with rage.
Aeneas fought the cruel king Mezentius instead, and defeated him. And the battle ended.
The next day, Aeneas sent the body of young Pallas home to his father, with a thousand soldiers to walk beside him. And old Evander wept for his son.

The Latins asked for a truce, so that they could bury their dead too. "You ask for peace for the dead," said Aeneas. "I would gladly give it to the living. I never wanted this war. It is Turnus who wants it. Let Turnus and I fight each other alone, and let the war be decided that way." For twelve days there was peace, and Trojans and Latins cut wood side by side on the hills.
In the city, many Latins were tired of the war. "Let Turnus fight Aeneas alone," they said. But before they could decide, the Trojans came marching across the plain.

Brave Camilla rode out to meet them with her horsemen. She fought like a whirlwind, and no one could stand against her. But a man named Arruns crept after her, waiting for his chance, and at last he threw his spear. Camilla fell from her horse. When she was gone, her horsemen fled, and the Latins ran back inside their city walls.

Now Turnus saw that everyone was looking at him. "Very well," he said. "I will fight Aeneas, man to man. Whoever wins will marry Lavinia." Lavinia blushed when she heard it, and Turnus loved her more than ever.

The next morning, both armies sat on the grass on either side of a field. King Latinus came in his chariot, wearing a crown with twelve golden rays, and Aeneas came in his shining armor, and they made a solemn promise: whatever happened in the fight, it would end the war.

But Juno would not give up. She sent Turnus's sister, a water nymph named Juturna, to stir up trouble. Juturna disguised herself as a soldier and walked among the Latins. "Are we going to let one man fight for all of us?" she said. Then she sent a sign: an eagle swooped down and caught a swan, but all the other birds chased the eagle until it dropped the swan. "Look!" cried a Latin prophet. "The gods are telling us to fight!" And he threw a spear at the Trojans. At once the promise was broken, and the battle began again.
Aeneas stood in the middle, with no helmet on, and held up his empty hands. "Stop!" he cried. "We made a promise!" But as he spoke, an arrow flew out of nowhere and struck him in the leg.

His friends helped him back to the camp. The arrowhead was stuck fast, and no one could pull it out. Then Venus secretly brought a magic healing herb from a mountain in Crete and stirred it into the water the doctor was using. As soon as he bathed the wound, the pain stopped, the arrow fell out by itself, and Aeneas felt as strong as ever. He put his helmet back on and returned to the battle.

Then Aeneas led his army straight to the walls of the city. When Turnus saw smoke rising from the towers, he jumped down from his chariot and ran toward the city. "Stop fighting!" he shouted. "Let me fight Aeneas alone, as we promised!" And at last the two heroes stood face to face.

They threw their spears. Their shields crashed together with a sound like thunder. Turnus struck a mighty blow with his sword, but it broke in half against Aeneas's shield, the shield Vulcan had made. In his hurry that morning, Turnus had grabbed the wrong sword! He turned and ran, and Aeneas chased him. Five times they ran around the field.
Up on Mount Olympus, Jupiter spoke to Juno. "How long will you fight against the Fates, my wife? You have chased the Trojans over land and sea. You have started a terrible war. Now it must end."

"I give up," said Juno at last. "But grant me one thing. Let the people of this land keep their own name and their own language. Let them be called Latins, not Trojans. Let Rome rule the world, but let the name of Troy be forgotten."

Jupiter smiled. "You are as fierce as ever," he said. "But I grant it. The Trojans and the Latins will become one people, and they will all be called Latins. And no people will honor you more than they will."

Then Jupiter sent a dark spirit that flew in front of Turnus in the shape of an owl, beating its wings against his shield. Turnus shivered with fear. His sister Juturna knew the sound of that owl, and she knew the end had come. She left her brother and dived sadly into her river.

Turnus picked up a huge stone, so big that a dozen ordinary men could not have lifted it, and threw it at Aeneas. But his strength was gone, and it fell short. Then Aeneas threw his great spear. It flew like a whirlwind, and struck Turnus, and he fell to his knees.
"You have won," said Turnus. "Everyone has seen it. Lavinia is yours. But if you have any pity for my old father, let me go back to him."

Aeneas stood still with his sword raised. He began to feel sorry for Turnus, and he almost let him go. But then he saw, across Turnus's shoulder, the gold-studded belt of young Pallas. And he remembered his friend, and his anger blazed up again. "Pallas strikes this blow, not I!" he cried. And that was the end of Turnus.

So the war was over. And just as the gods had promised, Aeneas married Lavinia, and the Trojans and the Latins became one people. Aeneas built a city and named it Lavinium, after his wife. Thirty years later, just as Father Tiber had promised, his son Ascanius built a new city called Alba, the White City. And from the family of Aeneas, many, many years later, came the twin brothers Romulus and Remus, who would build Rome.

A simplified retelling of Alfred J. Church's “The War in Latium” in Stories from Virgil (1879). The original is listed under Other versions only when “Show stories with mature themes” is on in Settings. Church spells the hero's name “Æneas” and calls Ascanius “Iülus.”
